name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

names.name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Beings are born to one of two endowments: the divine, marked by twenty-six qualities from fearlessness to absence of excessive pride (16.1–3), and the demonic, marked by hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance (16.4). The divine leads to release, the demonic to bondage (16.5). There are two creations of beings, divine and demonic (16.6); the demonic are described at length — their view of the world (16.8), insatiable desire and cares (16.10–12), self-conceit (16.13–15), sham sacrifice and hatred of the Lord in all bodies (16.17–18) — and their fate: hell (16.16), demonic wombs and a lower course (16.19–20).

name: The five causes of action (BhG 18.13–15)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Every action undertaken with body, speech or mind, right or wrong, has five causes, declared in the sāṃkhya (18.13): the seat (adhiṣṭhāna), the agent (kartṛ), the various instruments (karaṇa), the many distinct activities (ceṣṭā) and the divine (daiva) as the fifth (18.14–15); this being so, one who sees one's self alone as the agent does not see (18.16), and one whose disposition is not shaped by the sense of 'I' does not slay though slaying and is not bound (18.17).

notes: The verses do not explain the five; commentators' glosses (the body as seat; the senses as instruments; daiva as presiding deities, unseen merit or the Lord) are theirs.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The teaching is 'knowledge more secret than the secret', to be reflected on fully before the hearer does as he wishes (18.63); its 'most secret' word is told because the hearer is dearly loved (18.64). The teacher asks whether it was heard with one-pointed thought and delusion destroyed (18.72); the disciple reports delusion destroyed by grace and resolves to act (18.73). Sañjaya heard it directly from Kṛṣṇa by the grace of Vyāsa (18.75).

name: The threefold austerity (tapas) of body, speech and mind

names.name: The threefold austerity (tapas) of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Austerity of the body: worship of gods, twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, non-harming (17.14). Of speech: non-agitating, true, pleasant and beneficial speech and the practice of recitation (17.15). Of the mind: clarity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of disposition (17.16). This threefold austerity with supreme faith and without desire for fruit is sāttvic (17.17); done for respect and with hypocrisy, rājasic, unstable and impermanent (17.18); done from a deluded notion with self-torment or to ruin another, tāmasic (17.19).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Arjuna asks the truth of each (18.1). Saṃnyāsa is laying aside desire-prompted acts, tyāga giving up the fruit of all acts (18.2). Some say action is to be abandoned as faulty, others that sacrifice, giving and austerity are not (18.3); Kṛṣṇa's settled view: these are to be done, giving up attachment and fruit (18.4–6). Relinquishment is threefold: abandoning allotted action from delusion is tāmasic (18.7), from fear of hardship rājasic (18.8), doing it as what ought to be done without attachment or fruit sāttvic (18.9). The relinquisher neither hates nor clings (18.10); the embodied cannot give up action entirely, so the relinquisher of fruit is the tyāgin (18.11); the fruit of action accrues after death to non-relinquishers, not to renouncers (18.12). Through renunciation one attains the supreme perfection of freedom from action (18.49).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The actions of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras are distributed by the guṇas arising from their own nature (18.41); the brāhmaṇa's work born of nature is calm, restraint, austerity, purity, patience, uprightness, knowledge, discernment and faith (18.42); the kṣatriya's heroism, vigour, steadiness, skill, not fleeing in battle, generosity and lordliness (18.43); the vaiśya's agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade, the śūdra's service (18.44). The verses do not say whether 'nature' is fixed by birth.
